title: What financial sandboxes do for new businesses
label: · Financial sandboxes
summary: Four financial technology founders described very different experiences of regulatory sandboxes: some used them to test a product while preparing for permission to operate, while others sought guidance on rules for new kinds of financial services. The witnesses said sandboxes can help firms test ideas, build regulator relationships and sometimes progress more quickly towards authorisation, but the benefits and processes vary widely. They called for clearer aims, better feedback and more opportunities to learn together. One witness described a particularly clear route from sandbox testing to full authorisation; others said the link was uncertain or that the regulator did not actively check their progress.

glossary.definition: A supervised programme where a financial business can test a product or service under agreed limits.
The Financial Conduct Authority, which regulates financial services firms in the UK.
A system that lets customers securely share their bank-account information with approved services.
UK rules requiring financial firms to act to deliver good outcomes for their customers.
Official permission from a regulator to carry out specified financial activities.
A firm authorised to issue electronic money and provide related payment services.
Artificially created information used to test a product without using real customers' data.
A digital token designed to keep a steady value, often by being linked to a currency.
Financial investments, such as bonds, represented and managed using digital records.
The boundary between activities that financial regulation covers and those it doesn't.

chapters.title: Why the firms joined
chapters.takeaway: The businesses entered sandboxes for different reasons, from getting permission to operate to testing a new product with regulatory guidance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To start, why did you join a sandbox, and has it met your expectations?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: Relace builds technology to help firms understand and meet regulatory requirements. We joined to learn what the FCA expects under Consumer Duty, which is new and affects many parts of a business. Firms are struggling to gather the information they need, and we wanted to build something that could help.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: We joined because our tax software used open banking, and we needed permission to use bank-account information in that way. We thought the sandbox would be quicker than applying for full regulation directly. It wasn't mainly about testing something new; we needed a route to permission.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: We wanted regulatory guidance for issuing and settling financial securities using digital records. We couldn't just build first and ask questions later: this involves the capital markets. We looked for a regulator and a country willing to develop rules with the industry, and found the UK approach serious.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: Bourn was developing an alternative to business overdrafts. Our product involved payments and potentially holding customers' money, so we knew we needed permission. We chose to apply directly rather than operate as an agent of another authorised firm, because we wanted to build our own controls and credibility with banks.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: Some written evidence says there are no clear measures of success and that sandboxes don't lead properly to authorisation. Does that match your experience?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: Yes, the lack of agreed success measures rings true. We set our own targets: build a product, work with industry partners and be ready to launch. No one from the sandbox team agreed those targets with us or checked our progress. We offered to show what we'd built, but weren't taken up on it.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: We got the regulation we needed and left the sandbox successfully. But I had expected more of a shared experience with the other firms and hoped it might help us connect with financial institutions. I don't think it achieved that. The broader aim should be to help new businesses work with established firms and grow.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: Our experience is different. In the programmes we're in, the aims and route to permission are clearly set out, and the regulators are developing policy with industry. That won't be true of every sandbox, though; ours are focused on digital securities and stablecoins.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: For us, there was a connection to authorisation. We first received restricted permission to test, then applied to remove the restrictions when we left. It took about six months to get both permissions, and around a year including the sandbox testing. We think that was faster than applying directly.

turns.speaker: Lord Hill of Oareford
turns.text: Did the sandbox itself make authorisation quicker, because the regulator already knew your business?

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: I think so. We met the FCA's innovation team about once a month. We showed that the product worked and customers responded well, while also building the controls needed to operate fully. We didn't see exactly how that fed into the permissions decision, but the process felt connected.

chapters.title: The work involved and what firms can test
chapters.takeaway: Applying can take substantial time, while the support and testing conditions differ considerably between programmes.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bowles of Berkhamsted
turns.text: How much time, money and outside help did your applications require?

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: We spent about three months preparing an application of more than 100 pages, with help from a part-time compliance officer. We were only three founders at that point. It was hard work, but much of it—writing our plans and procedures—was work we'd need for authorisation anyway.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: It took a lot of time and focus for our small, bootstrapped team. We couldn't afford outside advisers, so we read the rules, asked the regulators questions and prepared the application ourselves.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: Our initial form took about five hours, but approval took another five months. Getting accepted didn't mean we could start testing: we still had to prepare a detailed business plan and registration documents. That took around 80 to 100 hours. It was worthwhile work, but the steps weren't obvious.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: Once testing began, we could serve about 200 people under limited permission. The tax year gave us a deadline: we needed to be ready for the January filing period. Once we saw that the service worked, we moved quickly towards full permission.

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: Our application took less time because we were clear about the problem and what we wanted to test. A former sandbox participant helped us informally, and a pre-application meeting with the programme lead helped us check whether our idea was suitable.

turns.speaker: Lord Lilley
turns.text: What does being in a sandbox actually allow you to do?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: We could use artificial datasets, such as made-up customer complaints, to test our software. We also got some cloud-computing credits, coding support and mentors with experience in areas like data protection, banking and intellectual property.

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: The mentors were especially helpful. What was missing was regular access to a senior expert in Consumer Duty. Over four months we had two short meetings with someone on that subject. A knowledgeable contact who took an active interest would have helped us much more.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: The word 'sandbox' covers very different things. In our case, the main benefit was limited permission to serve a small number of people—not access to test datasets. We need to be clear about what each programme is for.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: We didn't receive data from the regulator; we supplied simulated data to demonstrate our systems. In one programme, we met the FCA team weekly or every two weeks to discuss our technology, procedures and compliance. Another, run with the Bank of England, is longer-term and less intensive.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: We followed a detailed test plan, covering the product launch, customer feedback and whether the service could handle growth and technical problems. The FCA met us about monthly. Those meetings let it monitor the test and helped both sides understand the business.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: Could a simple waiver of some rules do the same job, without a sandbox?

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: Not for us. The digital securities programme gives us room to test activities that existing rules don't readily allow. A sandbox can be a controlled place where the regulator watches what happens; a waiver alone may not provide that ongoing discussion.

chapters.title: Learning, partnerships and business benefits
chapters.takeaway: Firms and regulators can learn from each other, but participants reported uneven follow-up and mixed evidence of lasting commercial advantage.

turns.speaker: Lord Eatwell
turns.text: Sandboxes are meant to reduce the risk that a regulator will reject a new idea after a firm has invested heavily. Did you find the regulators learned from you as well?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: There were only two group meetings for our cohort, at the start and midway through. Otherwise, firms worked separately. We asked to meet other participants whose work might connect with ours, but weren't introduced. We also offered feedback to the sandbox team, but I can't say whether it was used.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: Regulators learning from the businesses they supervise is essential. They also need to explain what a firm gets in return for spending time helping the regulator understand a new idea. Otherwise, a firm may help establish a market and then face competitors as soon as it gets permission to operate.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: In our case, both sides are learning. We can improve our processes, while the regulators develop the rules. We've made suggestions and seen some reflected in policy. We aren't authorised yet, so we can't say the sandbox has sped that up, but we may be better prepared.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: Our discussions felt genuinely collaborative. The FCA introduced us to its open banking specialists, and it seemed interested in what we were doing with data and artificial intelligence. It also publishes examples of innovation, which helps share what it learns.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Fforestfach
turns.text: Has being in a sandbox helped you raise money, attract staff or win business?

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: It helped us show investors and banks that our product had been tested and that we were ready to grow. We partnered with Investec and NatWest Group, which also invested in us. Around the time we left the sandbox, we raised £3.5 million in seed funding.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: We haven't raised money yet, so I can't say it helped with that. It has let us engage with regulators while the rules are being developed, which may give us a temporary information advantage. I don't think it creates a lasting advantage once the rules are in place.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: I don't know whether the sandbox gave us a direct advantage. We did something new with bank data and tax returns, but we weren't sure investors or large financial firms understood what the sandbox meant. Useful lessons about how open banking could help accounting also seemed to get lost.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: One wider cost is insurance. Because our service combines accounting and financial services, our insurance premiums are about 20 times what they would be for either activity alone. That cost is part of trying something new.

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: The publicity and trust have helped us find firms and customers willing to take a chance on an early-stage product. We built our product during the four months in the sandbox. It's useful, although it's too early for me to judge whether it gives us a lasting advantage.

turns.speaker: Lord Hill of Oareford
turns.text: Can you point to examples where a sandbox led regulators to change the underlying rules?

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: I can't give an example from a sandbox. Before sandboxes existed, I worked with the regulator on early electronic-money rules. That work helped shape the rules, but it wasn't part of a sandbox.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: I can't name a specific company whose sandbox changed a rule. But the rules for our area are still developing, and we've seen changes that reflect discussion with the industry. Different businesses may disagree about those changes.

chapters.title: What should change, and how the UK compares
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses urged clearer programme goals and more active support, while describing the UK's approach as more tangible than some alternatives.

turns.speaker: Lord Davies of Brixton
turns.text: What did you mean by saying some programmes amount to 'innovation theatre', or that the word 'sandbox' has become confusing?

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: In some places we applied or held discussions but received little follow-up. They invited firms and announced programmes, but we couldn't see a clear route from acceptance to permission or a lasting industry. The UK has been more convincing to us because it is developing rules and a route to operate, not just announcing a programme.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: I should say that 'innovation theatre' was another witness's phrase. But large companies can be enthusiastic about innovation while failing to follow through with small firms. As for sandboxes, people often talk about their benefits without knowing what a particular programme actually does.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: The sandbox gave banks a safer way to work with a very young business. We partnered with two banks while taking part, and I'm not sure they'd have taken the same chance without that structure.

turns.speaker: Lord Davies of Brixton
turns.text: Do you know how the FCA chooses which firms to accept? Is it even-handed?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: I don't know. We submitted a project proposal but weren't told why it was selected.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: I don't know either. We were using bank data to prepare tax returns, which was new at the time, and were encouraged to apply. I don't know what else was considered.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: We were rejected when we first applied in 2020, then accepted into later programmes. I can't explain the selection criteria. The sandbox helped us build credibility with established firms, but our application was a gamble.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: The FCA published criteria, and we tried to address them in our application. We weren't given feedback on the strengths or weaknesses of our bid.

turns.speaker: Baroness Donaghy
turns.text: Would it help to define the different types of sandbox, or should the financial sector stop using the word altogether?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: Defining the purpose would help. A technology provider like us needs different support from a firm seeking permission to provide a financial service. There should also be more chances for participants to share ideas and give feedback, and access to experts who understand the issue they're testing.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: The word is confusing, and the report shouldn't ignore that. If people use the same label for very different programmes, they may expect the wrong thing. What matters is matching the support to the programme's goal.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: It may be better to think of them as different innovation programmes, each with its own goals and requirements. In our case, there wasn't an ordinary route to permission for what we were building, so a programme to test it and develop rules was necessary.

turns.speaker: Baroness Donaghy
turns.text: But is every sandbox really about innovation? Some may just test whether a business can do something that already exists.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: Clearer names might help firms understand what they can apply for. Perhaps an earlier support or supervision programme could serve businesses before they reach the stage of the existing sandbox.

turns.speaker: Lord Smith of Kelvin
turns.text: What did you find when you looked at other countries?

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: We looked at the Netherlands, where a limited exemption may allow small-scale tests. That could be another option besides a sandbox.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: We also took part in Ireland's programme. These experiences weren't entirely negative, but we sometimes couldn't tell what would happen after acceptance. In the UK, we've had a fair chance to work alongside major firms, which we don't think we could have done everywhere.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: We looked at Belgium because we were uncertain how long the UK process would take. We could quickly speak to the regulator there and discuss the process, which was a positive experience, although we didn't apply in the end.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. That concludes the session.
